rv.q: So there’s almost a prelapsarian innocence to this loopy, postwar cartoon of England. But on to the tickle-feather of a plot: Famished and broke Francis hires himself out to two “guvnors” (bosses).
If you’re not having a good time at this show, you may be on the wrong medication.
Mr. Corden's Francis is a walking appetite, a man whose rumbling stomach dictates his every move, and he makes this primal motivation both hilarious and touching.

The slapstick farce and British vaudevillian merriment galloping throughout the exuberant music-hall comedy, 'One Man, Two Guvnors,' are a perfect fit for Corden's range of expressive comedic abilities.
James Corden is a whirling dervish of comic energy in this knockabout British farce, which transfers to Broadway with most of its National Theatre cast intact.

James Corden is a marvel of physical comedy and vocal dexterity, turning what could be a one-note farce into something approaching theatrical magic.
The young British actor headlining the London import is so mad talented, adorable and hilarious that you just want more of him.
It's undoubtedly the funniest, most insane show you'll find this season.
Guvnors often has you hoarse from laughing, and allows you the rare chance to brag about seeing something extremely tony that also happens to be incredibly Benny.
One Man, Two Guvnors is smart, it’s charming, and most importantly, it’s very funny!

Led by the roly-poly and irresistibly droll Corden – an ebullient performer clad in mismatched checks as the modern-day Harlequin figure –a skilled 16-member ensemble whips through a wacky progression of pratfalls, slapstick nonsense, cheeky doings and assorted other low-comedy capers.
